scenes.tts: The first film changed whole-chromosome dose. Can a chromosome rearrangement matter when no DNA seems missing? Follow the same coloured blocks through breakage and meiosis.
scenes.caption: The first film changed whole-chromosome dose. Can a chromosome rearrangement matter when no DNA seems missing? Follow the same coloured blocks through breakage and meiosis.
scenes.visual: Link directly to the first film. Rebuild its large blue and gold homologues in the same positions, then divide each into labelled blocks A through E. Break the blue chromosome between blocks while the total-dose gauge remains green. Put the question above the break. Keep fragments drifting slightly but visibly aligned. Reuse the exact colour map: blue = one homologue, gold = the other, teal = moved segment, green = balanced dose, red = extra or missing dose, grey = spindle and cell structure.
scenes.narration: The first film changed whole-chromosome dose. Can a chromosome rearrangement matter when no DNA seems missing? Follow the same coloured blocks through breakage and meiosis.

scenes.visual: Title card after the hook: Break, Rejoin, Segregate. Behind it, the blue chromosome's separated blocks slowly slide toward new positions.

scenes.tts: A chromosome is more than a counted object. Its blocks carry genes, and their order provides context. For any rearrangement, ask what material changed dose, what breakpoint changed context, and what products meiosis can make.
scenes.caption: A chromosome is more than a counted object. Its blocks carry genes, and their order provides context. For any rearrangement, ask what material changed dose, what breakpoint changed context, and what products meiosis can make.
scenes.visual: Enlarge one blue block chromosome until it fills most of the frame. Transform three small corner labels into a vertical checklist: DOSE, CONTEXT, MEIOSIS. As each is named, a dose gauge, a breakpoint marker and a spindle icon grow from the carried chromosome instead of appearing as disconnected chips.
scenes.narration: A chromosome is more than a counted object. Its blocks carry genes, and their order provides context. For any rearrangement, ask what material changed dose, what breakpoint changed context, and what products meiosis can make.

scenes.tts: Remove one block and the chromosome has a deletion. Its genes now have lower dose. A missing segment cannot supply its genes. Copy one block and the chromosome has a duplication. Those genes now have higher dose. An extra segment supplies another copy. The red gauge tracks both changes.
scenes.caption: Remove one block and the chromosome has a deletion. Its genes now have lower dose. A missing segment cannot supply its genes. Copy one block and the chromosome has a duplication. Those genes now have higher dose. An extra segment supplies another copy. The red gauge tracks both changes.
scenes.visual: Start with blocks A-B-C-D-E. Lift C out and leave a visible gap that closes into A-B-D-E; the red gauge moves to MISSING. Restore the original, duplicate C, and insert the copy beside it; the gauge moves to EXTRA. Mark the block model 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Remove one block and the chromosome has a deletion. Its genes now have lower dose. A missing segment cannot supply its genes. Copy one block and the chromosome has a duplication. Those genes now have higher dose. An extra segment supplies another copy. The red gauge tracks both changes.

scenes.tts: Now cut out several blocks and return them in reverse order. That is an inversion. No block is lost, so dose can stay balanced. The chromosome count also stays unchanged. During meiosis, homologous blocks bend into a loop to align.
scenes.caption: Now cut out several blocks and return them in reverse order. That is an inversion. No block is lost, so dose can stay balanced. The chromosome count also stays unchanged. During meiosis, homologous blocks bend into a loop to align.
scenes.visual: Cut blocks B-C-D from the blue chromosome, rotate the group, and reinsert it as D-C-B. Keep the dose gauge green. Bring in the straight gold homologue. Bend both chromosomes into a large loop until matching lettered blocks align. Do not show crossover products; the text works them out.
scenes.narration: Now cut out several blocks and return them in reverse order. That is an inversion. No block is lost, so dose can stay balanced. The chromosome count also stays unchanged. During meiosis, homologous blocks bend into a loop to align.

scenes.tts: A reciprocal translocation exchanges segments between nonhomologous chromosomes. Move a teal end segment from blue to a grey chromosome, and return a grey segment. Total dose may stay balanced even though both chromosomes have new neighbours.
scenes.caption: A reciprocal translocation exchanges segments between nonhomologous chromosomes. Move a teal end segment from blue to a grey chromosome, and return a grey segment. Total dose may stay balanced even though both chromosomes have new neighbours.
scenes.visual: Straighten the chromosomes. Add one grey nonhomologous chromosome. Break both at matching heights. Colour the blue end teal as it moves onto grey; move the grey end onto blue. The green total-dose gauge stays level. Highlight the two new block boundaries with pulsing white brackets.
scenes.narration: A reciprocal translocation exchanges segments between nonhomologous chromosomes. Move a teal end segment from blue to a grey chromosome, and return a grey segment. Total dose may stay balanced even though both chromosomes have new neighbours.

scenes.tts: Balanced dose does not guarantee no biological effect. A breakpoint can interrupt a gene block. It can also place pieces from different genes together. The result depends on which sequence meets the breakpoint. These are changes in gene context, not whole-chromosome count.
scenes.caption: Balanced dose does not guarantee no biological effect. A breakpoint can interrupt a gene block. It can also place pieces from different genes together. The result depends on which sequence meets the breakpoint. These are changes in gene context, not whole-chromosome count.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one generic labelled GENE block at a breakpoint. Split it without claiming a specific outcome, then show a second schematic possibility where half of GENE A sits beside half of GENE B. Label both 'can'. Keep the chromosome count counter unchanged and the dose gauge green. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Balanced dose does not guarantee no biological effect. A breakpoint can interrupt a gene block. It can also place pieces from different genes together. The result depends on which sequence meets the breakpoint. These are changes in gene context, not whole-chromosome count.

scenes.tts: The carrier still faces meiosis. Normal and translocated partners must align matching blocks. All four chromosomes form a cross-shaped group. The way this cross separates decides whether each gamete receives one copy of every block.
scenes.caption: The carrier still faces meiosis. Normal and translocated partners must align matching blocks. All four chromosomes form a cross-shaped group. The way this cross separates decides whether each gamete receives one copy of every block.
scenes.visual: Zoom back out. Bring in the normal blue and grey partners beside both translocated chromosomes. Rotate and connect matching block sequences into a large cross that fills the frame. Four gamete zones open around it. Thin grey spindle fibres attach from opposite poles and continue moving gently.
scenes.narration: The carrier still faces meiosis. Normal and translocated partners must align matching blocks. All four chromosomes form a cross-shaped group. The way this cross separates decides whether each gamete receives one copy of every block.

scenes.tts: Which separation preserves one copy of every coloured block: opposite chromosomes moving together, or neighbouring chromosomes moving together? Look at the block ledgers.
scenes.caption: Which separation preserves one copy of every coloured block: opposite chromosomes moving together, or neighbouring chromosomes moving together? Look at the block ledgers.
scenes.visual: Overlay two schematic arrow choices on the cross. Green dashed arrows connect opposite chromosomes; red dashed arrows connect neighbouring chromosomes. Put a question mark in each gamete zone. Do not reveal block counts.
scenes.narration: Which separation preserves one copy of every coloured block: opposite chromosomes moving together, or neighbouring chromosomes moving together? Look at the block ledgers.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Hold both arrow choices and keep only subtle spindle motion.

scenes.tts: Opposite partners preserve one copy of every block. This alternate segregation makes normal or balanced gametes. Neighbouring partners give each gamete an extra copy of one segment and no copy of another. This adjacent segregation makes unbalanced gametes.
scenes.caption: Opposite partners preserve one copy of every block. This alternate segregation makes normal or balanced gametes. Neighbouring partners give each gamete an extra copy of one segment and no copy of another. This adjacent segregation makes unbalanced gametes.
scenes.visual: Animate the green opposite arrows first. Move the appropriate chromosomes into paired gamete zones; a block ledger beside each lists the blue blocks A through E and the grey blocks, one copy of each, and turns green. Reset the cross completely. Then animate the red neighbouring arrows; each adjacent-segregation ledger shows one block doubled (for example teal twice) AND one block missing (for example the grey end absent); both ledgers turn red.
scenes.narration: Opposite partners preserve one copy of every block. This alternate segregation makes normal or balanced gametes. Neighbouring partners give each gamete an extra copy of one segment and no copy of another. This adjacent segregation makes unbalanced gametes.

scenes.tts: That explains a common puzzle. A carrier can be healthy because their chromosome set is balanced. Yet meiosis can produce unbalanced gametes. Balance must therefore be tested at both levels. The rearrangement's consequence depends on breakpoint context and segregation, not chromosome count alone.
scenes.caption: That explains a common puzzle. A carrier can be healthy because their chromosome set is balanced. Yet meiosis can produce unbalanced gametes. Balance must therefore be tested at both levels. The rearrangement's consequence depends on breakpoint context and segregation, not chromosome count alone.
scenes.visual: Bring the balanced carrier's chromosomes back to the centre with a green ledger showing one copy of each block. Below, fan out the alternate and adjacent gamete ledgers. Keep the carrier icon neutral, not labelled unaffected. Add a small 'outcomes can differ' label beside the breakpoint marker.
scenes.narration: That explains a common puzzle. A carrier can be healthy because their chromosome set is balanced. Yet meiosis can produce unbalanced gametes. Balance must therefore be tested at both levels. The rearrangement's consequence depends on breakpoint context and segregation, not chromosome count alone.

scenes.tts: Trace three things after every break. Ask what material was gained or lost. Ask which genes were interrupted or newly joined. Then ask which chromosome combinations can pass through meiosis. Rearrangements matter through DNA dose, gene context, and meiotic balance.

scenes.visual: Transform the dose gauge, breakpoint bracket and cross-shaped pairing group into one horizontal causal path. Let the balanced carrier ledger remain above it. End with the teal moved segment travelling through the path from BREAK to CONTEXT to MEIOSIS.
scenes.narration: Trace three things after every break. Ask what material was gained or lost. Ask which genes were interrupted or newly joined. Then ask which chromosome combinations can pass through meiosis. Rearrangements matter through DNA dose, gene context, and meiotic balance.
